ending: The voyage ends in three blows. On June 1, 1868, Nemo stops over the wreck of the Avenger, the French ship that sank rather than surrender to the English on that date in 1794. That same afternoon a warship flying no flag opens fire. Nemo raises his black flag, declares himself "the law" and "the tribunal," and at dawn on June 2 rams the ship below the waterline. He watches it sink with all hands, then kneels sobbing before the portrait of a woman and two children. For the first time we see both the crime and the wound behind it.

After that the Nautilus loses its way, and so does the book. The ship runs north for perhaps fifteen or twenty days. No positions go on the chart, no crew appear, and Aronnax loses count of the days. The scientist who listed every fish now cannot say which sea he is in. Verne openly brings in Poe's Arthur Gordon Pym, and the realism of the voyage gives way to nightmare. Ned is close to madness. When he finds land in the mist, escape is no longer a plan. It is the only way to survive.

Nemo's last words come in the dark lounge, where he has been playing the organ: "O almighty God! Enough! Enough!" Aronnax wonders if it is "a vow of repentance," and the book never says. Then the crew start shouting "Maelstrom!" and the skiff is torn loose. Aronnax says the Nautilus was steered into the whirlpool "accidentally—or perhaps deliberately." That leaves open whether Nemo, crushed by what he has done, set out to die. The narrator is knocked out at the crucial moment, so even the survival of the three friends happens off the page.

The Conclusion is all questions. Did the Nautilus survive? Is Nemo alive, and still taking revenge? Will his sealed manuscript ever wash ashore? Will the warship's nationality reveal his own? Aronnax answers with a hope, not a fact. He hopes the scientist outlives the executioner and that contemplating the sea's wonders will "extinguish the spirit of vengeance." The last line puts the two men side by side, the only humans who can answer Ecclesiastes' question about the depths. It is a strange tribute to a man who has just drowned hundreds of sailors, and Verne means the strangeness.

Verne did answer the questions later, though not quite in a way that fits. In The Mysterious Island (1874–75), castaways on a Pacific island are helped by an unseen protector who turns out to be an old, dying Nemo. The Nautilus survived the Maelstrom and is hidden in a sea cave. Nemo reveals that he is Prince Dakkar of India, who fought the British in the rebellion of 1857 and lost his wife and children to them. He dies aboard his ship, and the cave becomes his tomb. The dates in the two books do not match, and many readers prefer the open ending of this one. Here Nemo stays what his name says: no one.

themes.text: Wonder carries the book to its very last line, but the ending puts it under strain. After the massacre, Aronnax says, observing and classifying "were out of the question." His last tour of the museum is a farewell to a collection he expects to sink with its curator. Still, wonder is what he trusts to save Nemo, and the book ends by claiming the depths for the two men who have seen them. Verne's science is sometimes wrong: no sea is 16,000 meters deep, and there is no open water at the South Pole. But the habit of looking closely and naming what you see is the book's real subject.

Freedom never comes by permission. Nemo refuses to free his guests to the end. Escape comes only when the ship and its master have fallen apart, and only through the Maelstrom, a vortex from which, Aronnax says, no ship has ever escaped. The Conclusion turns the book's terms around. Nemo, who praised the sea as the one free place, ends the voyage as the prisoner of his grief and hatred. The prisoners walk away free, rescued not by their own plans but by chance and a fisherman's hut.

The book refuses to explain Nemo. We learn why he hates (homeland, wife, children, father and mother destroyed) but not who he is or who did it. Even the warship's flag is kept from Aronnax: "so much the better," Nemo says. The clues point in different directions, from the portraits of Kosciusko, O'Connell and John Brown to the French cry of the crewman taken by the squid. Verne's own drafts made him a Polish noble, and his next book made him an Indian prince. Within this novel Nemo stays a type more than a person: anyone whose country was crushed by a stronger power.

The hidden grievance finally comes into the open, and the book treats it with uncomfortable fairness. Nemo's suffering is real and his cause sounds just, yet the sinking of the warship is described as a slaughter, a "human anthill" drowned, with Aronnax pressed to the window. The Avenger, a ship that chose to die rather than surrender, is Nemo's model. His "Enough!" may mean he has seen where revenge leads. Aronnax holds both sides: whatever Nemo suffered, he "had no right to mete out such punishment," and yet his destiny is "sublime."

The sea has the last word. Nemo's rule over the ocean ends in the Maelstrom, a natural force his machine can only resist "like a human being," its steel cracking. Nature decides who lives, and the Conclusion can only say the skiff survived somehow. Aronnax's final hope is that the sea itself, Nemo's "adopted country," will heal what people did to him. The ocean is both the cause of wonder and an indifferent power that people do not control.

The Nautilus ends as what the world first feared: a monster that sinks ships. The book that explained every valve and battery now shows the spur going through a warship's hull "like a sailmaker's needle through canvas." Verne admires the machine and makes it plain that its meaning depends on who steers it. In the last chapters no one seems to steer at all. The hatches open and close by themselves, the course is random, and the most advanced ship on earth heads blindly into a whirlpool. Aronnax still hopes for "progress," but the book has shown its costs.

Nemo's escape from civilization fails, because he brings its worst habit with him. The man who mocked the idea of "savages" becomes judge and executioner, waging the same kind of war he fled. His black flag at the Pole and on the platform is the flag of a nation of one. Meanwhile Aronnax returns to the human world. He is taken in by poor Norwegian fishermen, and he waits for a steamboat with his notes and a story he fears no one will believe.

The three companions began as a set of comic types and end as friends. In the last days Conseil keeps a constant watch over Ned, afraid he will kill himself. Ned plans the escape and stocks the skiff, and when he vows to fight to the death, Aronnax answers, "Then we'll die together." They wake in the hut "clasping my hands." Nemo's crew show a darker loyalty: some fifteen men share their captain's hatred on the platform, and whatever became of the Nautilus, they share its fate, bound to their captain to the end.

interpretations.title: Persecutor or persecuted?
interpretations.text: Aronnax asks this question halfway through, and the ending refuses to settle it. Some readers see Nemo as a freedom fighter in a world of empires, and the sinking as an act of war by a man whose people had no other means. Others see a terrorist who murders sailors with no say in their government's crimes. Verne gives both readings weight. Nemo has Aronnax's sympathy and sometimes his admiration, but the massacre is shown in full and called by its name. The book does not ask you to forgive him. It asks you to understand what made him.

interpretations.title: An anti-imperialist hero in an age of empire
interpretations.text: Nemo's heroes are rebels against empire: Kosciusko for Poland, Botzaris for Greece, O'Connell for Ireland, Manin for Italy, John Brown and Lincoln against slavery. His gold goes to Cretans rising against Ottoman rule. Read with the later Prince Dakkar in mind, the unnamed warship looks British and the book becomes an attack on the greatest empire of the day. Postcolonial critics also note the limits. Aronnax calls the Papuans "savages," Nemo claims the South Pole in his own name like any explorer, and the hero who resists empire is still a European-style aristocrat with a museum full of Western art. The book is against oppression without being free of its time's assumptions.

interpretations.title: No one: Nemo and Odysseus
interpretations.text: "Nemo" is Latin for "no one," the name Odysseus gives the Cyclops in the Odyssey to escape him. The echo fits a sea voyage full of monsters and wonders, but it also changes the story. Odysseus uses the name for a moment to escape the Cyclops. Nemo takes it forever to give up home and identity entirely. Readers have also linked him to the Romantic rebel figures of Byron and to Prometheus: a genius who defies the world's powers with stolen fire, here electricity, and pays for it alone.

interpretations.title: The cozy enclosure: Barthes on the Nautilus
interpretations.text: In his essay "The Nautilus and the Drunken Boat" (in Mythologies, 1957), Roland Barthes argued that Verne's real dream is not adventure but shelter: a perfectly closed, well-stocked interior from which to watch the vast world through a window. The Nautilus, with its library, organ and cigars, is the ultimate comfortable room. Seen this way, the long lists of species are the point, not padding: they turn the ocean into an inventory. The ending, where the ship loses all bearings and is cracked open by the whirlpool, is the dream breaking.

interpretations.title: Prophet or teacher?
interpretations.text: Verne is often called a prophet of the submarine, but real submarines already existed, and he knew it. His ship shares its name with Robert Fulton's Nautilus of 1800, a real early submarine. His aim was to teach. The novel first appeared in Hetzel's Magasin d'éducation et de récréation, a magazine meant to educate young readers, and its catalogues of fish and figures are lessons dressed up as adventure. Some readers find the lists a drag. Others think they are the heart of the book: a celebration of knowledge as something you can enjoy.

context.title: The Polish captain Hetzel would not allow
context.text: In Verne's early plans Nemo was a Polish nobleman whose family had been killed by Russian forces, a clear nod to the crushing of the Polish uprising of 1863. His publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, objected: the Russian market mattered, and the book might be banned there. Verne argued hard, and the compromise was silence: Nemo's nation and his enemy are never named. That is why the book's central mystery has no solution. Kosciusko's portrait, first among Nemo's heroes, may be a trace of the original plan. In The Mysterious Island (1874–75) Verne gave Nemo a new past as Prince Dakkar, an Indian rebel against the British, an enemy Hetzel had less reason to protect.

context.title: Research, a model submarine and a suggestion from George Sand
context.text: The novelist George Sand wrote to Verne in the mid-1860s hoping he would take his readers into the depths of the sea. He did his homework. He read oceanography and natural history, and at the Paris Exposition of 1867 he could see a model of the French Navy's submarine Le Plongeur. The world of the book is the world of the late 1860s: the transatlantic telegraph cable laid in 1866, the Suez Canal under construction (it opened in 1869), the uprising in Crete. Some of Verne's science reached beyond what was known. Nobody reached the South Pole until 1911, and it lies on a high ice plateau, not by an open sea.

context.title: The Voyages Extraordinaires
context.text: The novel belongs to Verne's Voyages Extraordinaires, the series of more than fifty novels he wrote for Hetzel, beginning with Five Weeks in a Balloon (1863). Hetzel's stated goal was to sum up all the geographical, geological, physical and astronomical knowledge of modern science in entertaining form. Twenty Thousand Leagues ran as a serial in 1869–70 and came out in two volumes. The title measures distance traveled, not depth: twenty thousand leagues is about 80,000 kilometers, roughly twice around the world.

context.title: A famously bad translation
context.text: For about a century most English readers met the book in the 1872 translation credited to "Mercier Lewis," a pen name of the Reverend Lewis Page Mercier. It cut close to a quarter of the text, including much of the science, and was full of mistranslations and garbled numbers. This helped give Verne a reputation in English as a writer of boys' adventure stories. Scholars led by Walter James Miller began exposing the damage in the 1960s. Complete modern translations, such as William Butcher's (1998) and F. P. Walter's (1999, the text this app follows), restored the full book, including its politics and its learning.

adaptations.title: 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea
adaptations.note: Stuart Paton's silent film for Universal, which mixed in The Mysterious Island and pioneered real underwater photography.

adaptations.title: 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea
adaptations.note: Disney's Technicolor version, directed by Richard Fleischer, with James Mason as a haunted Nemo and Kirk Douglas as Ned Land. It won Oscars for art direction and special effects, and its ornate Nautilus became the standard image of the ship.

adaptations.title: Mysterious Island
adaptations.note: A loose version of the sequel with Ray Harryhausen's stop-motion creatures and Herbert Lom as Nemo.

adaptations.title: 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea: Submarine Voyage
adaptations.note: A Walt Disney World ride based on the 1954 film, in which guests rode Nautilus-style submarines through a lagoon. It closed in 1994.

adaptations.title: 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea
adaptations.note: One of two rival television films made the same year. This one starred Michael Caine as Nemo.

adaptations.title: The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen
adaptations.note: Alan Moore and Kevin O'Neill's comic series has Nemo, as an Indian prince, among a team of Victorian fictional heroes.

questions: Nemo says the warship's crew destroyed his homeland and family. Does that change how you judge the sinking? Is there anything he could have done to those men that you would call justice?
Why do you think Verne kept Nemo's name and nation hidden, even after Hetzel's objection forced his hand? Would the book be stronger or weaker if we knew?
What do you think Nemo meant by "Enough! Enough!"? Did he steer the Nautilus into the Maelstrom on purpose?
Aronnax calls Nemo's destiny "sublime" just after watching him drown a ship's crew. Is this admiration a moral failure, or honesty about how fascinating Nemo is?
Ned, Conseil and Aronnax respond to captivity in very different ways. Whose response did you sympathize with most, and did that change during the book?
Nemo protects right whales but slaughters sperm whales, and loves the sea while using it as a weapon. How consistent is his idea of nature?
Did the long lists of species and scientific explanations add to the book for you, or get in the way? What do you think Verne wanted them to do?
The book admires the Nautilus and fears it. Which modern technologies raise the same mix of feelings, and who controls them?
